title: Assistant Professor
bio:
Dionne Bennett is an Assistant Professor in the African American Studies Department. She holds a Ph.D. in Anthropology from the University of California, Los Angeles where she studied in the Psychocultural Studies and Medical Anthropology Program, and she graduated Magna Cum Laude with a B.A. in Anthropology and Literature from Yale University. She was previously the Director of the African American Studies Program at the University of Detroit Mercy and an Assistant Professor of African American Studies and a Visiting Professor of Women's Studies at Loyola Marymount University. She has been a fellow of Harvard University's W.E.B. Du Bois Institute for African and African American Research, the Ford Foundation, and the UCLA President's Office. She has been an associate of the The Hiphop Archive at Harvard University since its founding in 2002 by Marcyliena Morgan, Ph.D. She is the author, with photographer Matthew Jordan Smith, of Sepia Dreams: A Celebration of Black Achievement through Words and Images, co-editor of Revolutions of the Mind: Cultural Studies in the African Diaspora Project 1996-2002 (CAAS Publications, University of California Los Angeles, 2003), and a contributor to Black Los Angeles: American Dreams and Racial Realities (NYU Press, 2010).

She has served as a consultant to California Literacy, Inc., the nation's largest state-wide adult literacy organization and was the principal investigator for the organization's study of health literacy. As a television writer, researcher, and segment producer, she has worked for the NAACP Image Awards, the Essence Awards, the Democratic National Convention, and the Fox Movie Channel. Her research interests include African American and African Diaspora Studies, urban anthropology; psychocultural anthropology, media and cultural studies; critical and comparative race theory; women's and gender studies; the study of sexuality, desire, and emotion; and Hiphop culture, which, of course, combines all of the others.

Debarati Biswas is Assistant Professor of African American Studies and Coordinator of the Black Visual Cultures Minor. Her academic interests include contemporary Black and U.S. Ethnic literary and aesthetic practices; Queer and Trans of Color Critique; Black and third world feminisms; Marxist theory; critical theories of race and subjectivity; and migration studies. Her book project tentatively titled "The Perpetually Unsettled:  Aesthetics of Elsewheres and Queer Politics in Black American Literature and Culture, 19542018" explores the affective and embodied dimensions of blackness and queerness in carceral spaces such as the prison, inner city, and single room occupancy hotel.  Work from her dissertation on Black queer embodiment in single-room occupancy hotels was published as the co-written article “Rituals of Survival in Single-Room Occupancy Hotels” in Social Text, Duke University Press in 2024. She also co-edited a special issue of WSQ: Women's Studies Quarterly titled “Unbearable Being(s)” in 2024. Her writing also appears in venues such as Public Books and Teen Vogue; as well as in the anthology, The Parasitical Logic in Culture and Society, edited by Peter Hitchcock and published by Bloomsbury Academic. She also coproduced an award winning docu-fictional webseries, Three Trembling Cities, on immigrants of color in NYC. Biswas serves on the Editorial Board of WSQ: Women’s Studies Quarterly and is the Co-Chair of the Board of Directors at CLAGS: The Center for LGBTQ Studies at the Graduate Center, CUNY. She is also the 2025-2026 Faculty Fellow at The Center for Place, Culture, and Politics at The Graduate Center, CUNY.

title: Professor
bio:
Teaching Expertise: Black women and girls’ cultural and literary narratives; African American migration narratives; the history of Black theatre and performance; and the Africana experience in New York City.

Marta Effinger-Crichlow, Ph.D is the author of Staging Migrations Toward an American West: From Ida B. Wells to Rhodessa Jones by University Press of Colorado. Her other writings are included in The Routledge Companion to African American Theatre and Performance, Debates in the Digital Humanities, African American Lives, Theatre Journal, African American Review, Footsteps: Children’s Magazine, Journal of Black Studies, and the Dictionary of Literary Biography. Effinger-Crichlow is also a dramaturg, playwright, and documentary filmmaker. Produced works include the multi-media collage The Kitchen is Closed Startin' Sunday and Whispers Want to Holler, which included a collaboration with noted jazz saxophonist Billy Harper.

Effinger-Crichlow, who was AFR Chair from 2011-2021, also served as the project director and co-investigator for CityTech’s first National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) grant project entitled Retentions and Transfigurations: The Technological Evolution and Social History of Five New York City Neighborhoods. This NEH funded faculty development initiative was designed to strengthen the teaching of humanities within technical and professional studies programs.

Effinger-Crichlow is currently on the advisory board for The Black Theatre Review (tBTR), “a biannual online, peer-reviewed journal published by the Black Theatre Network (BTN).” In 2020, The Craft Institute invited Effinger-Crichlow to offer her theater course entitled Digging into Black Life and the Black Archive. She has also been an invited lecturer at The Rosie the Riveter Museum of the National Park Service in Richmond, CA; Syracuse University; New York University’s Gallatin School; The African Burial Ground Museum and Monument of the National Park Service in New York City; Lane College’s NEH Summer Institute in Eugene, OR; and Xiamen University in China. She serves as an advisor on the feature documentary Chocolate Milk (dir. by Elizabeth Bayne). In 2015, she appeared on TEDxCUNY at the TriBeCa Performing Arts Center in New York City. In 2014, The Network Journal, which recognizes "Black women leaders and influencers in every field," selected Effinger-Crichlow as one of their "25 Influential Black Women in Business."

Effinger-Crichlow’s feature-length documentary film project is LITTLE SALLIE WALKER. It tells the story of a diverse group of Black women and girls who depend upon childhood play to survive girlhood and even womanhood in America. Recognition for the film project include the 2022-2023 Fellow, DOC NYC x Video Consortium Incubator; 2022 Fellow, WIF x Sundance Intensive; 2022 Grant Recipient of the New York City Women’s Fund for Media, Music and Theater; 2021 Recipient, DOC NYC's Only in NY Program; 2021 Fellow, Cucalorus WiP Lab; 2021 Athena Works-in-Progress Program; The Perspective Fund; 2020 Working Films Impact Kickstart; 2019 DCTV Lab; Lower Manhattan Cultural Council/New York Dept. of Cultural Affairs Engagement grant; New York Council on the Arts-Individual Artist grant; New York Women’s Foundation grant; PSC-CUNY Enhanced and Trad. B. grants; 2017 IFP JustFilms Ford Foundation Fellow at the Made in NY Media Center; and a Women Make Movies Production Assistance Program recipient.

title: Associate Professor
bio:
Javiela Evangelista is an Associate Professor in the African American Studies (AFR) Department. As a public anthropologist she engages in participatory research that counters inequalities, at the intersections of citizenship and racialization in the Caribbean and the African Diaspora.

Evangelista’s book manuscript is an ethnographic analysis of the largest case of mass statelessness in the western hemisphere, the contemporary denationalization of Dominicans of Haitian descent in Dominican Republic. Support has been received by Harvard University’s  Mahindra Humanities Center, Andrew Mellon Foundation, Social Science Research Council, and Center for Place, Culture, Politics and People.

Evangelista’s work has been featured at the Venice Biennale and in the Publication of Afro-Latin/American Research Association (PALARA), National Political Science Review and Interdisciplinary Team Teaching (Palgrave).

She serves on the Advisory Board of Futures Initiative and on the Editorial Board of Women Studies Quarterly. At City Tech, Evangelista is co-chair for the Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) Steering Committee; co-chair of Assessment for the School of Arts and Sciences; and the AFR course coordinator for Caribbean Studies

PhD, Anthropology, Graduate Center, CUNY
MA, Institute for Research in African American Studies, Columbia University

title: Chair
bio:
Renata Ferdinand is a Full Professor and Chair of the Department of African American Studies at NYC College of Technology in Brooklyn, NY.  She graduated from Fort Valley State University before earning an M.A. in English and a Ph.D. in Communication Studies from Bowling Green State University in Bowling Green, OH.

Her work has been featured in several outlets, including Girlhood Studies (2022), Cultural Studies + Critical Methodologies (2022;2018), Journal of Health Psychology (2016), and The Popular Culture Studies Journal (2015) as well as within several book chapters. She has written the foreword and back-of-book blurbs for both student anthologies and academic books, served as a manuscript reviewer for Louisiana State University Press and University of South Carolina Press, and served on the editorial board for the Journal of Mother Studies, Journal of Autoethnography, and The Autoethnographer: A Literary and Arts Magazine. In 2023, she was awarded a $25,000 grant from the Black, Race, and Ethnic Studies Initiative (BRESI) for programming highlighting Black and Latinx Girlhood. She has served on dissertation committees both in the U.K and the U.S.A. She was recently awarded two writing residencies: In Cahoots in California and Wildacres Residency in North Carolina.

Research Interest:

My research focuses on functional foods and medicinal plants with health-promoting properties, particularly their roles in combating oxidative stress, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. I explore nutrient-rich and fortified foods, as well as traditional herbs like Ashwagandha, Shankhapushpi, and Shatavari, to understand their potential in preventing chronic diseases and supporting neuroprotective and metabolic health. My work emphasizes the biochemical and cellular mechanisms underlying these effects, utilizing both in vitro models and nutritional interventions. This research integrates aspects of nutrition, pharmacology, and endocrinology to address complex health challenges, including obesity and age-related decline. Through this interdisciplinary approach, I aim to contribute to the development of evidence-based dietary and therapeutic strategies for long-term health and wellness.

Research Interests:

  • My research focus is on the molecular basis of neurodegenerative diseases like Dystonia, and Parkinson's. Deletion of a single glutamate in torsinA correlates with early-onset Dystonia, the most severe form of a neurological disorder, characterized by uncontrollable muscle contractions. Symptoms usually begin around age 12. The disorder typically begins in just one part of the body, but it eventually spreads to other regions and leaves individuals severely disabled and confined to a wheelchair. My aim is to find out, how the abnormal version of the protein torsinA, leads to the disease.

Research Interests:

  • Intracellular protein degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway is a highly complex and tightly regulated process. It plays important roles in a variety of basic cellular processes. Among them are the regulation of cell cycle and division, involvement in the cellular response to stress, modulation of cell surface receptors, DNA repair, biogenesis of organelles and regulation of the immune and inflammatory responses. Aberrations in protein degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway have been implicated in the pathogenesis of many diseases, such as cancer, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease, etc. Our research mainly focused on the molecular basis underlying the involvement of this pathway in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's diseas and Alzheimer's disease. Further studies in this field may bring us new insights into the pathogenesis of these diseases and provide therapeutic alternatives for these devastating disorders.

title: Professor
bio:
Dr. Diana Samaroo, Professor of Chemistry, was recently named City Tech’s 2022 - 2023 Scholar on Campus. City Tech will honor Dr. Samaroo on Wednesday, May 4, starting at 5:00 p.m., in the New Academic Building, 285 Jay Street in room A-105. The event is open to the college community, and it will be preceded by a reception in the lobby of the building.

Professor Samaroo has been a member of the City Tech faculty since 2009. After the completion of her doctorate in Biochemistry, she was a post-doctoral fellow at Weill Medical College of Cornell University. Dr. Samaroo’s research over the years spanned immunology, synthetic chemistry, molecular biology, and nanomaterials. She has worked on research projects that investigated the link between celiac disease and gluten, as well as schizophrenia. Applications of novel synthetic porphyrinoid-related compounds to photodynamic therapy and nanomaterials have been her main research focus. Porphyrin-type molecules that appended to sugars and amines are often designed to target cancer cells or disease-causing cells. She investigates their photophysical properties and cellular uptake. Dr. Samaroo’s research also seeks to address the molecular transport of these molecules and their interaction with proteins and DNA. Her pedagogical interests focus on integrating authentic research experiences inside and outside the classroom, peer led team learning and the retention and graduation of students in STEM.

Dr. Samaroo’s scholarly works have earned over 500 citations, and she has published over 25 peer reviewed articles and conference proceedings. She has famously co-authored an article on RNA probes for cell imaging with Nobel Laureate Eric Kandel, and she has written extensively on photophysical properties of chlorins for diagnostic and therapeutic applications and also on the immune response to gluten in patients with schizophrenia. Dr. Samaroo has considerable experience reviewing manuscripts for journals such as Future Medicinal Chemistry, Langmuir, Molecules, New Journal of Chemistry, and the Journal of Chemical Education. She served as a reviewer/panelist for the National Science Foundation (NSF) and for the PSC- CUNY. Dr. Samaroo is currently co-PI on several National Science Foundation (NSF) grantsthat include: NSF S-STEM, NSF HSI-IUSE and NSF RCN UBE, and she is also the Project Director for a grant from the Robin Hood foundation that focuses on supporting first yearstudents. Dr. Samaroo served as co-PI on a previous NSF S-STEM grant, as well as senior personnel on a National Institute of Health grant. Thematically, these grants create opportunities for undergraduate student success by providing scholarships, academic student support, and authentic research experiences.

Additionally, Dr. Samaroo served as Chairperson for the Department of Chemistry for six years. For numerous years, she diligently served on the Undergraduate Research Committee, the Assessment Committee and on College Council. With colleagues, she co-organized two major conferences that were held at City Tech – SENCER Mid-Atlantic Regional Conference and the 13th Annual Black Male Initiative Conference. With the support of programs such as Honors and Emerging Scholars, CUNY Service Corps, and the Louis-Stokes for Alliance Minority Participation, Dr. Samaroo has mentored over fifty undergraduate students at the college, some of whom have been co-authors on her publications.

Professor Ferrell is an award-winning poet, a three-time finalist for the Joy Harjo Poetry Award, and a recipient of the Hedgebrook Artist In Residence Fellowship. Additionally, she serves as the Poetry Editor for Bellevue Literary Review (BLR). Her fourth poetry collection, bone, will be released in 2026 (NYQ Books). She is currently working on her next collection, bloodroot, which uses poetry and creative non-fiction to walk through the generations of her matrilineal familial line, in the hopes of finding the family’s first African matriarch brought to America in bondage.

Both her teaching and writing focus on issues of Womanism/Feminism, race, (C)lass, gender politics, sexuality, and representations of sexual identity. In her courses, Ferrell asks her students to examine their understanding of the growing global society alongside the antiquated paradigms that govern us all. Overall, whether composition or literature, students will find that Ferrell’s courses usually lend themselves to lively and animated discussions that focus on the politics, cultures, emerging technologies, social expectations/responsibilities, and ideologies that make us uniquely human.

More than anything, the bright spot of her time at the college has been watching the growth and development of her students as they become promising, thoughtful, and insightful young scholars.

English and Applied Linguistics ESOL Coordinator

Lubie Grujicic-Alatriste holds a doctorate in Applied Linguistics from Columbia University, Teachers College and an MA in Applied Linguistics and TESOL from the University of Surrey, United Kingdom.  She has presented around the world from Hong Kong and Australia to Europe, United States and Hawaii. Professor Grujicic-Alatriste’s research combines systemic-functional linguistics, composition and rhetoric studies, and second language acquisition. Her current work is in genre analysis of academic student and professional writing. At present Dr. Grujicic-Alatriste is researching student-generated argumentative compositions and is developing a theoretical taxonomy of  “school genres” – types of writing done by students and faculty within the academic discourse community. Her most recent textbook has applied the tenets of genre scholarship  to  more closely reflect the 21st century media, spoken and written genres for urban college writers.

bio:
Carole K. Harris received a B. A. in French Literature from Duke University (1984) and a Ph. D. in Comparative Literature from Yale University (1993). Before joining the English Department at City Tech, she has taught French, Comparative Literature, and English Composition at a variety of other institutions, including Yale University, Bennington College, Rutgers University, the University of California at Irvine, and Hofstra University. title: Professor
bio:
As a professor and higher education administrator, Dr. Hellman has long been invested in student access, equity, and excellence. As Interim Special Assistant to the President from 2022-2024, Dr. Hellman played a crucial role in strategic planning and institutional advancement. She oversaw the Office of Communications, cultivating a sense of belonging and connection for the current and extended college community; providing vision for advertising and marketing campaigns to support enrollment initiatives; and collaborating with leadership across the College regarding critical internal campus communications.

Dr. Hellman has served as a professor in the City Tech English Department since 2007, with the exception of her time as a 2011 Fulbright scholar in American Literature at the University of Antwerp and her administrative leadership. At the University level, she has been a steadfast advocate for developmental education reform, and cofounded the CUNY Writing Discipline Council. A 2021-2022 CUNY Leadership Institute Fellow, Dr. Hellman has a long-standing commitment to public higher education. She holds a B.A. in English and Art History from Wellesley College and a PhD in English from the CUNY Graduate Center.

title: Professor
bio:
Dr. Reneta D. Lansiquot-Panagiotakis is Co-Advisor of the National Society of Collegiate Scholars (NSCS) Platinum Star Chapter at New York City College of Technology (City Tech), where she was named Scholar on Campus. She is Co-Founding Director of the Interdisciplinary Design Game-Based Learning Lab, which she established with Prof. Tamrah D. Cunningham, where she leads honors students in designing narrative-driven educational digital and non-digital games to support learning across disciplines.

A proud City Tech alumna, she earned her A.A.S. in Computer Information Systems and her B.Tech. in Computer Systems, and initiated City Tech's NSCS Chapter with Dr. Janet Liou-Mark, growing it from a student initiative into a nationally recognized Platinum Star Chapter (2025-2026), ranked in the top 10 among 300+ chapters nationwide. In recognition of her leadership, she was named, alongside Prof. Cunningham, the 2021 NSCS Chapter Co-Advisor Team of the Year. She earned her M.S. in Integrated Digital Media from Polytechnic University (now NYU Tandon School of Engineering) and her Ph.D. in Educational Communication and Technology from New York University, where she has also taught undergraduate and graduate courses.

Her interdisciplinary studies include Literature and the Arts in Paris, Transnational Communities and Media Cultures in London, and British literature in its European Context in Cambridge, along with a certificate in Shakespearean Tragedies from the University of Cambridge, French as a Foreign Language from New York University, and TESOL from Teachers College, Columbia University. She is also a Certified Organization Advisor (COA) through the Leadership Excellence and Advisor Development (LEAD) program and a certified Web Accessibility Specialist.

Dr. Lansiquot-Panagiotakis' mixed-methods research spans interdisciplinary studies, including technical writing, mathematics education, science education, game design, virtual reality, and computational thinking, and she has presented her work at numerous national and international conferences across Austria, Canada, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Greece, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. She has authored peer-reviewed book chapters and journal articles in these areas and is the author and editor of several books, including Interdisciplinary Pedagogy for STEM: A Collaborative Case Study (2016), Technology, Theory, and Practice in Interdisciplinary STEM Programs (2016), Place-Based Learning in Urban Education: Exploring Virtual Worlds (2018, co-edited with Sean P. MacDonald), Interdisciplinary Perspectives on Virtual Place-Based Learning (2019, co-edited with Sean P. MacDonald), and Interdisciplinary Team Teaching: A Collaborative Study of High-Impact Practices (2020).

She has also served as a consultant for media and telecommunications companies as well as nonprofit organizations in Afghanistan and the United States. She previously served as Director of the Honors Scholars Program, Founding Program Director of the Bachelor of Science in Professional and Technical Writing , and Founding Chair of the College’s Interdisciplinary Committee.

Courses Taught:

Developed and co-taught interdisciplinary general education courses that integrate computational thinking, creative practice, and technical writing, including Programming Narratives and Weird Science. Also designed courses within the major focused on technical documentation and advanced technical writing. Additional teaching experience includes specialized communication for technology students as well as films from literature and composition courses. Courses are taught using a combination of partially online instruction and in-person active learning experiences, with game-based learning incorporated where appropriate.

title: Associate Professor
bio:
Jody R. Rosen, an assistant professor in the English Department at New York City College of Technology, holds an AB from Brown University and a PhD and Women’s Studies Certificate from the CUNY Graduate Center. As a Writing Across the Curriculum coordinator, she values the role of writing in all courses, and integrates writing-intensive and communication-intensive approaches into her composition and literature courses. Her scholarship focuses on narrative theory, Modernisms, and gender and sexuality studies. Her work has been published in the Virginia Woolf Miscellany and in Forces of Nature:  Natural(-izing) Gender and Gender(-ing) Nature in the Discourses of Western Culture.  She is currently working on a manuscript on 1920s women's fiction, in which she considers the function of repetition as a subversive narrative mode in marriage-plot revisions emerging from the post-World War I era, focusing on novels by H.D., Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Nella Larsen, Edith Wharton, and Virginia Woolf.

Saddik is CUNY Distinguished Professor of Theatre and Literature, with a dual teaching appointment at The Graduate Center Ph.D. Program in Theatre and New York City College of Technology Department of English. Specializing in 20th and 21st century drama and performance, particularly the work of Tennessee Williams, Dr. Saddik has published four books and serves as the Editor-in-chief of the Tennessee Williams Annual Review.  

Her most recent book, Tennessee Williams and the Theatre of Excess(Cambridge UP), contextualizes Williams’ plays through what she terms a "theatre of excess," which seeks liberation through grotesque exaggeration, chaos, and ambivalent laughter. Her other books include Contemporary American Drama (Edinburgh UP [U.K] and Oxford UP [U.S.]), an exploration of the performance of American identity on the stage since World War II; The Politics of Reputation: The Critical Reception of Tennessee Williams’ Later Plays (Associated University Presses/Fairleigh Dickinson UP), which was the first full-length study of Williams' post-1961 career; and The Traveling Companion and Other Plays(New Directions Publishing), a definitive edited collection of Williams’ previously unpublished late plays.  

In addition to publishing books and over 50 essays on theatre studies in numerous journals, critical anthologies, theatre programs, and encyclopedias of theatre history, Dr. Saddik lectures and advises on productions both nationally and internationally as a dramaturg. She has served as a Lucille Lortel Awards voter and participates regularly in audience "talk-backs" for Broadway and Off-Broadway performances. Awards include a 2019-2020 appointment as Honorary "Chair Professor" of the School of Foreign Studies (Hunan University of Science and Technology, Xiangtan, China); a 2018 Short-Term Guest Professorship at The Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt (Bavaria, Germany); Eastern Michigan University ’s 2015 McAndless Distinguished Professor Award; and the New York City College of Technology Scholar on Campus Award (2007).  

She is currently working on a new book that centers on the ambiguous figure of the grotesque clown, which serves as a site of transformation and possibility in plays that reacted to systems of oppression during the second half of the twentieth century.

Brief Bio:

Sean joined the City Tech English Department in 2010. Prior to arriving in Brooklyn, he lived in Iowa City, Iowa and taught English at the University of Iowa and Kirkwood Community College. He enjoys reading, writing, photography, running, cycling, and skiing. He lives with his family in Greenwood Heights.

Academic Interests:

Sean is the founder and editor of the City Tech academic journal NANO: New American Notes Online, an online peer-reviewed interdisciplinary publication. NANO publishes scholarly articles on special topics that range from navigation to digital humanities, from competition and play to the aesthetics of trash.

Sean’s teaching and research interests include: US and world literature, gothic culture and literature, New York City history and literature, professional editing, narration theory, science fiction, artificial intelligence, and homesickness.

Areas of Interest: American Literature and Culture after 1900, Intersectional Feminism, Queer Studies, Critical Trauma Studies, Gothicism, Medical Humanities

Laura Westengard (she/they) is an Associate Professor of English and Coordinator of the interdisciplinary Gender & Sexuality Studies Minor. She serves as Board Co-Chair of CLAGS: The Center for LGBTQ Studies, the first university-based LGBTQ research center in the United States, and sits on the Editorial Board for the journal WSQ: Women’s Studies Quarterly. Her book, Gothic Queer Culture: Marginalized Communities and the Ghosts of Insidious Trauma, was released in 2019 by University of Nebraska Press as part of the Expanding Frontiers series. The book shows how queer culture adopts gothicism to challenge heteronormative and racialized systems and practices and to acknowledge the effects of microaggression and insidious trauma on queer communities. She is also the co-editor of The 25 Sitcoms that Changed Television: Turning Points in American Culture and has published in journals such as JNT: Journal of Narrative Theory and Steinbeck Review. She is currently researching medical archives for an upcoming book on lesser known 19th and early 20th century medical devices that have shaped contemporary queer cultural production in the United States.

Research Interests:

I am interested in the interaction between prosodic structure and morphophonological information, particularly as it relates to Austronesian languages. On a featural and segmental level, I am interested in various types of fusion, especially nasal substitution in Malay. On the level of phonetics, I am concerned to see better databases created for languages for which there is little beyond anecdotal assessment of stress placement. My current research involves testing the predictive value of the prosodic structure I have proposed for Malay.

My secondary interest lies in the syntax of English, specifically as it relates to coreference and indexing in right node raising structures.

Research Interests:

My research work in recent years has focused on the analysis of written academic discourse by non-native postgraduate students of Spanish. Within the field of Applied Linguistics in Spanish language teaching, I have been interested in understanding the processes involved in academic text composition and rhetorical discourse organization. I center specifically on the rhetorical functions that the students use in their citations in academic texts and its relation with the different stances and voices in the text. I am also interested in Critical Discourse Analysis, Intercultural Rhetoric in relation to gender analysis, the heritage students' written productions, the study of the student's construction of writer identity, and the implication of politeness and persuasion through the analysis on the usage of metadiscourse in academic writing.

Dr. Henry Africk is a Professor of Mathematics at New York City College of Technology. He received his bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Columbia University, a master’s and doctorate degree in mathematics from the University of Illinois - Urbana, and a second master’s degree in electrical engineering with an emphasis in computer science from the NYU Polytechnic University. He was chair of the mathematics department from 1997 to 2014.

title: Professor
bio:
Urmi Duttagupta is a Professor in the Department of Mathematics at New York City College of Technology of The City University of New York (CUNY). She received her baccalaureate degree in mathematics from The Ohio State University and her MS and PhD in Applied Mathematics jointly from New Jersey Institute of Technology and Rutgers University. Her research interests include optimization, infectious disease modeling and graph theory applications on biodiversity problems. She was invited as a visiting research faculty by the Center for Discrete Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science (DIMACS) at Rutgers, the State University of New Jersey for 2011-2012. She was also a short term visitor at the National Institute of Mathematical and Biological Synthesis (NIMBioS) at University of Tennessee, Knoxville in 2011 and was also invited to participate in NIMBioS Investigative Workshop on algebraic mathematical biology in 2016. Prof. Duttagupta has numerous publications in peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, book chapter to her credit and is the recipient of several grants including two NSF S-STEM grants (2009, 2015), multiple MAA NREUP grants (2011-2016), a Living Lab Gen Ed Seminar fellowship (2012-2013), a SENCER leadership fellowship, The National Society of Collegiate Scholars Distinguished Member Award (2014), a CURM min-grant and two PSC-CUNY grants/awards. Prof. Duttagupta has extensive experience of mentoring about forty students through different programs such as the NYC-AMP program, City Tech’s Emerging Scholar Program, CRSP grants, and MAA NREUP grants. Besides working as a mathematician she enjoys writing and drawing. As a strong believer of “serving the greater good of humanity and the world” her writing or artwork often reflects social issues that matter to her. She loves nature and its colors. Her painting or writing frequently celebrates nature and its beauty. Many of her work also have geometric patterns or mathematical symbols, which signify her love for mathematics.

title: Professor
bio:
Nadia Stoyanova Kennedy is Professor in Mathematics Education in the Department of Mathematics and Program Director of Mathematics Education. She received bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Mathematics from Sofia State University, Bulgaria. Between completing her master's and doctoral degree, she was a full-time high school mathematics teacher for 15 years, a curriculum developer and a student teacher mentor. Before joining City Tech, she held a faculty position at the Department of Mathematics at Stony Brook University. She was the founding director of the New York City Men Teach Program@Citytech (NYCMT) and directed the program from 2016 to 2019.

She has published 5 textbooks, one book, and published over 50 refereed articles and chapters in numerous mathematics education journals, anthologies and conference proceedings. She has presented at more than 90 national and international conferences. She has given 43 invited presentations, among which three international conference keynote addresses. She has acted as a consultant for the International Baccalaureate Organization (IB) on curriculum, assessment, and examiner training since 2007.

She is the PI on the “My Brother’s Keeper Teacher Opportunity Corps II grant” of $1.3 M from NYSED (2023-2028), which provides tuition support and professional development to teacher candidates for the next five years. The grant will help create and support a pipeline of a diverse and talented teaching force for New York City Schools. She is also the Co-PI on an NSF S-STEM grant "Engaging, Empowering, and Retaining New Scholars in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics,” $999,625 (2019-2024), which supports, and helps retain and graduate academically talentedSTEM students.

Currently, she is a Faculty Research Associate for the CUNY Computer Science Integration in Teacher Education (CITE) Research Practice Partnership, and leads the City Tech Math Education Team, which is part of the CUNY Computer Science Integration in Teacher Education (CITE) — a four-year initiative to support CUNY faculty in integrating state standards and aligning computing content and pedagogy with CUNY teacher education programs.

title: Professor
bio:
Boyan Kostadinov is an Associate Professor at NYC College of Technology, CUNY. He joined the Mathematics Department in 2009. Prior to that, he held positions at Credit Suisse Securities as a fixed income research associate in the Global Modeling and Analytics Group, in London and New York. Before obtaining his Master in Finance from Princeton University, he was an Adjunct Assistant Professor of Mathematics at UCLA, after obtaining his PhD in mathematics from UCLA in 2005. His dedication to teaching was rewarded by receiving the prestigious Robert Sorgenfrey Distinguished Teaching Award from UCLA, awarded by Professor Robert E. Greene. Professor Kostadinov has a strong commitment to undergraduate student research and has been a faculty adviser to more than 40 students, who have given presentations at local, regional and national conferences. He is interested in real-world applications of mathematics as well as developing innovative teaching materials, using modern computational and visualization technology for creating dynamic documents using R, Python and Markdown. He is always looking for ways to understand, present and explain advanced mathematical concepts and phenomena through interactive visualizations, animations and computer simulations that build intuition and conceptual understanding, for both teaching and research.

title: Professor
bio:
Throughout his career as a physicist, Dr. Andrea Ferroglia focused his attention on the study of the fundamental building blocks of matter and their interactions, a field that goes under the name of Elementary Particle Physics. His activity consists in carrying out calculations to predict what is expected to emerge from particle collisions at high-energy colliders. In the last fifteen years, he studied primarily processes measured at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), located at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland, where the Higgs Boson was discovered in 2012. Most of Dr. Ferroglia's recent work dealt with the production of top quarks, the heaviest particles in the Standard Model of elementary particle physics. The study of this quark is particularly relevant since, due to its large mass, the top quark is likely to emit a Higgs boson. Consequently, the top quark is an ideal portal to study the Higgs field and its role in the electroweak symmetry-breaking sector of the Standard Model. In addition, he worked on various aspects of Quantum Electrodynamics (Bhabha scattering, electron-muon scattering), weak decays of the bottom quark, and technical aspects of Quantum Chromodynamics, such as Soft-Collinear Effective Theory.

The particle physics community is an international network of scientists; the effort to improve our understanding of the fundamental building blocks of matter is truly global. After receiving his PhD from New York University in 2002 and before joining City Tech, Dr. Ferroglia held post-doctoral positions at the University of Freiburg (Germany), Zurich University (Switzerland) and Mainz University (Germany), and over the years has presented his work in seminars and conferences at institutions in the US, Germany, Switzerland, UK, France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Poland and the UAE.

Dr. Ferroglia strives to communicate his enthusiasm for physics and his research in elementary particle physics to students at City Tech. He coauthored papers with two graduate students in high-energy physics at the City Tech Physics department, Dr. Zhang and Dr Sameshima. Thanks to the CRSP program, he mentored three students (two of which continued their studies at Boston University and Stony Brook University, respectively), and mentored numerous others in a variety of physics topics within the ESP program. Dr. Ferroglia continues to involve interested students in his research, leveraging his network of collaborators and connections with international institutions to bring students in contact with this vibrant and global research environment.

title: Chair
bio:
Dr. Giovanni Ossola is a theoretical physicist whose research has significantly contributed to the field of high-energy particle physics. He obtained his Ph.D. in Theoretical High Energy Physics in 2004 at New York University under the guidance of Professor Alberto Sirlin, a renowned expert in the study of electroweak interactions. Before joining the Physics Department at New York City College of Technology in 2008, he held postdoctoral research positions at the University of Turin, Italy, and at the NCSR “Demokritos” Institute of Nuclear and Particle Physics in Athens, Greece.

Dr. Ossola’s notable contributions to the research in particle physics include the development of the OPP (Ossola-Papadopoulos-Pittau) method, a new approach which greatly simplifies the calculation of complex multi-leg Feynman diagrams, a crucial tool for evaluating scattering amplitudes and comparing them with the experimental outcomes of particle interactions as studied at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Located at CERN in Switzerland, the LHC is the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator, capable of accelerating particles to nearly the speed of light and colliding them with immense energy. Physicists use the LHC to study the fundamental building blocks of matter and the forces that govern their interactions, allowing them to explore the mysteries of the universe at the smallest scales, including the search for new particles and the study of the properties of the Higgs boson. The OPP method has had a significant impact on particle physics research, making its way into current Quantum Field Theory textbooks.

Dr. Ossola has also contributed to the development of open-source computational tools for the evaluation of scattering amplitudes, publicly available to the whole particle physics community, such as CutTools (2008), Samurai (2010), and GoSam (2012-2016) and applied them to obtain testable predictions for numerous processes of interest in the study of electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions, such as “QCD Corrections to Higgs Boson Production Plus Three Jets in Gluon Fusion” (Physical Review Letters, 2013) or “Associated production of a top pair and a Z boson at the LHC” (Journal of High Energy Physics, 2017). Dr. Ossola has published over 40 articles in refereed journals, plus numerous conference proceedings. His body of work has earned more than 7000 citations. He has received numerous awards and grants in recognition of his contributions. Over the years at City Tech, he won four NSF research grants in particle physics (three as the PI and one as co-PI) and numerous PSC-CUNY awards, attesting to the high quality and significance of his research.

Dr. Ossola is a faculty member of the CUNY Graduate Center, where he has been teaching Quantum Mechanics for the first-year students since 2015 and has mentored several graduate students, including Ray Sameshima, a CUNY graduate student who successfully defended his thesis in 2019 under Ossola's guidance. Dr. Ossola is also the coordinator of the Qualifying Exam which all first-year graduate students at the CUNY Graduate Center must take before starting their research work.

In addition to his research contributions, Dr. Ossola has had a significant impact on the education of students at City Tech, by providing mentoring in undergraduate research, advisement, and high-quality teaching. He played a crucial role in the development of the bachelor program in Applied Computational Physics (ACP), which empowers students with the skills and knowledge needed to excel in a wide range of computational applications. The problem-solving and coding skills taught in the ACP program have applications that go beyond physics research, in a variety of industries as well as in finance. As the ACP program director and coordinator, he is an important presence and point of reference in the students' educational paths.

title: Associate Professor of Psychology
bio:
About

Dr. Amanda Lee Almond is a health psychologist whose scholarship centers on racial microaggressions in health care and higher education, with particular emphasis on how these experiences shape health outcomes, professional identity, and behavioral change. Her current research explores the measurement and mitigation of bias in clinical encounters, the emotional and structural consequences of gendered and intersectional microaggressions in academic psychology, and the promotion of self-care and health engagement among health service trainees. Methodologically, Dr. Almond employs a range of approaches, including psychometric scale adaptation and validation—such as the Racial Microaggression in Medical Practice Scale (RMMPS)—as well as qualitative and feminist methods like thematic analysis and mixed-methods concept mapping to integrate lived experience with empirical rigor. She frequently applies the Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change to understand and facilitate anti-racist practice in medicine, positioning readiness to change as a critical variable for both individual clinicians and institutions. Her most recent work this framework to evaluate and operationalize anti-racist behaviors in medical settings. Across these projects, Dr. Almond's interdisciplinary research bridges health psychology, critical race theory, and behavioral science to advance equitable care, structural accountability, and sustainable well-being in health professions and communities.

Current Research:

On January 25, 2011, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of Egyptian cities to end Egypt's longest running dictatorship in both modern and ancient history. "The people demand(ed) the end of the regime" of Hosni Mubarak, Egypt's president. The latest uprising in Egypt and its participation in the "Arab Spring" brought global attention to the country nestled in the western corner of Northern Africa. Movements in solidarity with Egypt sprung up as far as the American state of Wisconsin and the world watched as the bloody hand that ruled Egypt with an iron fist finally fell when Hosni Mubarak resigned. The history of modern Egypt is marked by such uprisings. Periodically, beginning in the mid-19th century, Egyptians gathered together in protest to assert their dissatisfaction with their subservient economic and social position as they watched western Europeans reap the rewards of their hard earned labor, the Suez Canal. This culture of protest would mark Egypt's modern history.
My book, Umm al Dunya: the Making of Modern Egypt will trace the political, social and cultural relationship between Egypt's people and its government and show that Egypt's position as a leader in the Arab world resulted from an uneven power relationship with Europe, local political corruption and an indigenous response that was rooted in class conflict.

title: Professor of Sociology
bio:
Diana Mincyte is a professor of sociology at the City University of New York’s New York City College of Technology. Trained in rural sociology and science and technology studies, she studies self-reliance, autonomy, and sovereignty in agri-food infrastructures. She is particularly interested in the labor dimensions of food systems, approaching these questions through the frameworks of social reproduction, care, drudgery, and automation. Her recent publications examine the role of care in industrial agriculture, social reproduction in agro-food economies, and family farming in the Baltic states. Her current research explores how competing visions of food sovereignty are negotiated in geopolitically vulnerable regions with a focus on Lithuania. Her work has received best publication awards and has been supported by grants and fellowships, including fellowships at the Rachel Carson Center at Ludwig Maximilian University in Munich, Germany; the Agrarian Studies Program at Yale University; the European Studies Center at Harvard University; and the Center for European and Mediterranean Studies at New York University.

title: Associate Professor of Economics
bio:
Prof. Nyambuu holds degrees from both Chinese and American universities and speaks four languages fluently (Mongolian, Russian, Chinese, and English). She received her bachelor’s degree in Economics with specialization in Money and Banking from Peking University in Beijing, China. Dr. Nyambuu completed her Ph.D. in Economics at the New School for Social Research in New York. Prior to joining City Tech, she was a Post-Doctoral Fellow in New York University’s (NYU) Finance and Risk Engineering Department (Tandon School of Engineering); she also taught at NYU’s School of Arts & Sciences, at The New School for Social Research, and at Parsons School of Design.

Before joining academia, Dr. Nyambuu worked for the Central Bank of Mongolia, advising banks on international business strategies and assessing economic policy. She managed trade-financing operations for and between Mongolian and Chinese banks. She worked with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and with the World Bank (WB), where she was involved in analyzing international financial flows and forecasting commodity prices. Later on, Prof. Nyambuu worked as a consultant for the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) in Vienna, Austria, and for the International Labour Organization (ILO), a United Nations affiliate based in Genève, Switzerland. As a practicing economist, her background includes not only extensive teaching and research experience, and international economic and financial analysis, but also work in banking and domestic business development.

In 2018, Dr. Nyambuu authored Globalization, Gating, and Risk Finance, published by John Wiley & Sons, Inc., together with co-author Charles Tapiero, who holds the Topfer Chair in the Finance and Risk Engineering Department, Tandon School of Engineering, NYU. This book seeks to create a greater awareness of the evolution of finance in an era of globalization and, increasingly, its gating, and introduces these effects into financial pricing, trade, and compliance modeling. The book discusses many facets of global finance, emphasizing some of its essential concerns and elements, and explores the compound problems that geopolitics, macroeconomics, and finance entail.

title: Associate Professor of Anthropology
bio:
Research Interests

My forthcoming book from Brill Publishing, Symbolic Traces of Communist Legacy in Present Day Hungary: Experiences of a generation that lived during the Socialist era, draws on postcolonial theory’s understandings of how past powers can later impact peoples at the margins. My book sheds light on how personal practices of an older working class generation symbolically refurbish elements from the Communist era to fit present-day issues and challenges. Topics include: gift exchange, foodways, folklore, healthcare, aging, popular culture, nostalgia, identity, migration, and politics. My article “Washing Machine Races, Gulag Pizza, and McLenin: Kitsch-fication in Post-Socialist Hungary” in Ethnos: Journal of Anthropology explores popular culture in the form of communist kitsch. A forthcoming article in Anthropos “Ritualization of Ethno-nationalism: A Textual Analysis of a Hungarian Corpus Christi Procession” uses a textual analysis to explore how the ritual mirrors post-socialist trends that affirm Hungarian identity. This peer reviewed article serves to both document an interesting ritual procession but also view it in light of growing ethno-nationalism that both unites a community yet also shows exclusion of others. It is like a mirror at a microcosmic level that reflects a kind of ritualization of ethno-nationalism. My ongoing research has benefited from having received PSC-CUNY awards to conduct fieldwork in Hungary during the summer (2011-2016). This work in progress focuses on life histories of elderly Hungarian women as they adjust to and reinterpret the societal constraints of Hungary’s Socialist era to global issues associated with post-socialism. I have interviewed elderly women to get a sense of the impact of the Socialist past on their everyday practices post-socialism and am currently transcribing the audio into text. I am exploring new media by using videotaped interviews that I hope to edit into a short documentary for classroom use.

title: Associate Professor of History
bio:
Parvaneh Pourshariati is Associate Professor of History in the Department of Social Sciences at the New York City College of Technology of the City University of New York (CUNY). A historian of Late Antiquity and the medieval Western Asia, her research examines the political, social, religious, and intellectual history of Iran and Western Asia from the Parthian and Sasanian periods through the rise of Islam and the early Abbasid era. Trained at Columbia University under Richard W. Bulliet, with a secondary specialization in European diplomatic history and the Eastern Question under Sir David Cannadine, she employs an interdisciplinary methodology that integrates historical, archaeological, numismatic, literary, and religious evidence.

Professor Pourshariati is internationally recognized for her pioneering reinterpretation of Late Antique Iran and Western Asia. Her landmark monograph, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire: The Sasanian-Parthian Confederacy and the Arab Conquest of Iran (I.B. Tauris, 2008), fundamentally reexamined the political organization of the late Sasanian Empire and transformed scholarly debates concerning the Arab conquest of Iran and the political and social structure of Iran in the context of Late Antiquity. The work has been translated into Persian and Arabic, with the Persian edition appearing in multiple printings and being selected among the finalists for Iran's International Book of the Year Award. Fred M. Donner described the book as "a monumental work of first-class scholarship"; Stephen Dale characterized it as "a major, even pathbreaking, work"; and Hugh Kennedy called it "the most important re-examination of late Sasanian and early Islamic history since Christensen." Her publications span Sasanian political in the context of Western Asian Late Antiquity bringing together the Byzantine the Arab and early Islamic Histories, the Arab conquests ((628-), the Abbasid Revolution (750s, Iranian religious movements, Mithraism, the history of Iranian Jewry, Iranian and Arabic historiographies, the Shāhnāmeh (the Book of Kings tradition). Her recent work includes studies on Mithraic inscriptions and religious traditions in northeastern Iran, the Mazdakite movement, and the historical geography of Ctesiphon and Baghdad. She is currently completing several book-length studies on Trade and the Arab Conquests of Western Asia (650s) and the Abbasid Revolution (750s), Epic productions of the eastern Iranian world in Late Antiquity, Iranian Jewry and the rise of Islam in the context of Late Antiquity, as well as the rebellion of Babak Khorramdin in Azerbaijan which was about to topple the ʿAbbasids.

Before joining CUNY in 2014, Professor Pourshariati taught for fourteen years at The Ohio State University/Columbus as Professor of Islamic and Iranian Studies, following appointments at the University of Michigan and the University of Massachusetts. At OSU she taught graduate courses on

• Popular Epic Romances of the Iranian World
• When Mihr Met the Christ, Mani Met St. Augustine, and the Magi Met the Rabbi: Pre-Islamic Iranian Religions and their Legacies
• Religious Movements of Mesopotamia and Iran circa 600-750
• The ‘Abbasid Revolution: Muslim Narratives of Upheaval
• Narratives of Origin: The Islamic Tradition
• Rise of Islam and the World of Late Antiquity: Merchants and Ideologies
• The Arabs, the Byzantines, and the Sasanians: Cultural and Historical Currents in Late Antiquity (History/Persian 721)
• Narratives of Conquest and their Human Environment: The Arab Conquest of Iran (NELC/History 792)
• Major Themes in 'Abbasid Historiography History (727)

She has held distinguished research fellowships and visiting appointments at the Institute for the Study of the Ancient World at New York University, the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and as a Lady Davis Fellow at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Earlier in her career, she was the Shaykh Hamad Abdullah Muhammad al-Thani Fellow and Assistant Curator of Islamic Coins at the American Numismatic Society.

Professor Pourshariati served as President of the Association for the Study of Persianate Societies and serves on the editorial boards of several international journals. She has been a Founder and Director (2022- ) the Founder and Director of the Circle for Late Antique and Medieval Studies (CLAMS) at CUNY/GC and New York City College of Technology, -- an interdisciplinary research forum that brings together leading scholars from around the world through lectures, workshops, and international collaborations. Her research has been supported by fellowships and grants from the Social Science Research Council, the American Association of University Women, PSC-CUNY, the Iran Heritage Foundation, and the Center for Iranian Studies at Columbia University.

At City Tech, Professor Pourshariati teaches courses on Western Civilization and Islamic Civilization while pursuing an active research agenda that seeks to rethink major historical narratives through the integration of textual, archaeological, and material evidence. Her work continues to shape international scholarship on the Iranian ecumene in Late Antiquity, the Sasanian Empire in the context of Western Asian Late Antiquity, medieval Western Asian History.

Current Research:

Drawing on theory from the fields of personality psychology, social psychology, positive psychology and the psychology of religion, my research interests explore the concepts of identity conflict and integration in lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ) people of faith. My work has a strong applied focus that directly relates to such culturally salient issues as political ideation, religiosity/spirituality, fundamentalism, authoritarianism and tolerance/intolerance. Other underlying themes include social justice, identity development, social identity theory, stress-related growth and individual/institutional empowerment. I am currently focusing my research efforts on expanding my theoretical ideas regarding sexual and gender minority people of faith through my ongoing involvement with the LGBTQ Muslim Experience Study, the LGBTQ People of Faith Working Group and the Identity Integration Measure Project. Future research plans include: 1) teaming with student researchers to continue analyzing the large amount of qualitative and quantitative data I have collected to date, 2) constructing instruments that more accurately measure identity conflict and integration between religious beliefs and sexual orientation, 3) conducting an even larger survey study of LGBTQ people of faith, and 4) exploring the connection between faith, sexual orientation, positive psychology and the “Big Five” personality traits.

title: Associate Professor of History
bio:
Biography

Dr. Geoff D. Zylstra is a historian whose work studies the relationship between industrial change and the built environment in nineteenth-century cities, particularly Philadelphia and New York City. His research examines how diverse groups engaged in social and political struggles over the meaning and form of emerging technologies. His current project explores the racial desegregation of Philadelphia’s streetcars in the mid 1800s.

His scholarship has been published in numerous journals, including Technology and Culture (where he also serves as a Contributing Editor), the Journal of Urban History, and the Journal of Urban Technology. He also contributed to developing public policy through research on the history of poverty for the U.S. House Committee on Ways and Means.

Dr. Zylstra has significant experience with national-level grant work. He received a National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) grant for the project Making Connections: Engaging the Humanities at a College of Technology. This initiative helped inspire the development of the NEH’s “Humanities Connections” program, which promotes interdisciplinary links between the humanities and other fields. He previously worked on three NEH-funded projects focused on the Brooklyn waterfront and collaborated with the Brooklyn Historical Society on Students and Faculty in the Archives, supported by the U.S. Department of Education’s Fund for the Improvement of Postsecondary Education (FIPSE) .

His public history work includes contributions to the History Channel program, 101 Inventions That Changed the World, and as a volunteer advisor to the Friends of the Howe House in New Jersey.

While his primary teaching focus is at New York City College of Technology, work that he feels passionate about, Dr. Zylstra has been invited numerous times to teach in the graduate program at New York University’s Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development.

Areas of Interest

North American social and cultural history, history of technology, urban history, environmental history, and history of science.

title: Associate Professor
bio:
Professor Anzalone is a licensed Architect and Principal in the Brooklyn firm Atelier Architecture 64, with built projects locally as well as nationally and internationally. His professional work seeks to integrate the practice of architecture with the academic subject that Professor Anzalone teaches: advanced materials and systems, digital design, analysis & fabrication, new modes of construction, and design for adaption.

Professor Anzalone's research includes the incorporation of advanced science and technology into the architectural practice, design and construction. His work has included advanced materials and building systems, building integrated solutions, deployable / adaptable / temporary constructions and the study of the space and methods of making. In order to test his theories, Professor Anzalone has built twelve installations in nine different countries exploring how work can be developed and deployed in unfamiliar and uncertain situations. These projects have served as case studies for his research into automation techniques in site-work, designing for temporary or changing conditions, and developing adaptable structures. Professor Anzalone has authored extensive journal papers, chaired symposium, developed patented systems, participated in grants and constructed full-scale prototypes in his areas of research.

Profesor Anzalone is a member of the America Institute of Architects, a Board Member of the Association for Computer Aided Design in Architecture, and on the advisory board for a number of industry and academic partners.

Professor Anzalone's past academic career has included a ten-year appointment at Columbia University's Graduate School of Architecture, where he was the Founding Director of the Laboratory for Applied Building Science (formerly the Digital Fabrication Lab) as well as the Director of the Building Science and Technology Department. Professor Anzalone lead research and curriculum at the Lab, taught core graduate courses in architectural technology, as well as provided consulting for numerous creative constructed projects at the School and with industry partners.

Professor Anzalone has been awarded a Bachelors of Professional Study in Architecture from SUNY Buffalo and a Masters of Architecture from Columbia University. Past experience include work as an architectural designer with Greg Lynn Form and a facade consultant with R. A. Heintges and Associates.
